title: Peter’s denial of Jesus. Part 1
scripture_text: ‘’Then Jesus told them, “This very night you will all fall away on account of me, for it is written: ‘I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered.’ But after I have risen, I will go ahead of you into Galilee.” Peter replied, “Even if all fall away on account of you, I never will.” “Truly I tell you,” Jesus answered, “this very night, before the rooster crows, you will disown me three times.” But Peter declared, “Even if I have to die with you, I will never disown you.” And all the other disciples said the same…..Now Peter was sitting out in the courtyard, and a servant girl came to him. “You also were with Jesus of Galilee,” she said. But he denied it before them all. “I don’t know what you’re talking about,” he said. Then he went out to the gateway, where another servant girl saw him and said to the people there, “This fellow was with Jesus of Nazareth.” He denied it again, with an oath: “I don’t know the man!” After a little while, those standing there went up to Peter and said, “Surely you are one of them; your accent gives you away.” Then he began to call down curses, and he swore to them, “I don’t know the man!” Immediately a rooster crowed. Then Peter remembered the word Jesus had spoken: “Before the rooster crows, you will disown me three times.” And he went outside and wept bitterly.’’
devotional:
In post-Depression America, thousands of young servicemen and civilians streamed to arenas to see the programs, which included preaching, music, and various acts. One of the leaders in this movement was a young man from Canada, Charles Templeton, born in 1915. He was generally acknowledged to be the most versatile of the new young evangelists. Templeton soon rose to prominence, even surpassing another dynamic young preacher, Billy Graham. In 1946, he was listed among those ‘best used of God’ by the National Association of Evangelicals. In 1996 in his autobiography, Farewell to God, Charles Templeton lists his ‘reasons for rejecting the Christian faith.’

We are all familiar with the story of how Peter denied Jesus three times, it is one of the few stories that is recorded in all the four gospels. The reasons why all four Gospel writers may have included this story is to warn us that we have all got the potential to be like Peter and deny Jesus. It’s one thing to start the Christian race, but it is quite another to finish it. Sadly none of us has any guarantee of finishing the race well. We all know people who started off on the Christian life, and now they live far from God. We want to look at Peter’s denial and hope we can learn some lessons from it.

Peter would have been the last person others would have expected to deny Jesus; he was the most prominent of all the disciples. Often he expressed his desire to follow Jesus, even lay down his life for Jesus. If we had not known that Jesus had said that Peter would deny him three times, we would have all been surprised or even shocked by his denial.

Peter’s denial of Jesus is a concentrated example of denial. When we read about how Peter denied that he knew Jesus, it is very stark, very blatant, and it gives the appearance of happening suddenly.

I doubt few of us have denied Jesus in such a public and forceful way. There is a temptation to distance ourselves from Peter’s experience. However, the elements that went to make up Peter’s denial are found in every denial of Jesus, but they may not be as blatant.

What does it mean to deny Jesus? And what does denial look like?

The best way to answer that question is to get Jesus’ perspective on denial, to try and see it the way He does.

When Jesus predicts Peter’s denial the first thing Jesus tells Peter and the rest of the apostles that. “This very night you will all fall away on account of me.’ (Matthew 26:31.) When Jesus speaks of falling away he is thinking of these men being caught in a trap. The word used for ‘fall away, is skandalon from where we get our English word scandal. Skandalon in Greek literally meant the wooden stick that would hold up one edge of a metal box-trap. Food would be put under the box. An animal would be tempted by the food to enter the trap. Then the hunter would stay a significant distance away, hidden from view. The hunter would then use a small string that was holding the skandalon stick. The hunter would pull on the string, causing the skandalon stick to collapse. The box-trap would fall, and the animal’s whole body would normally be trapped inside. The animal would be skandlised.

In other words, denial of Jesus is an expression of being trapped.

When we loose our freedom and become enslaved to something we are denying Jesus his rightful place.

The word also carries the idea of being offended or ashamed about someone else, as we shall see shortly, Peter may have been feeling ashamed, disappointed and confused about Jesus when he denied him.

Jesus uses a second word that gives us more insight into how He perceives denial. Speaking to Peter Jesus said, “I tell you the truth this very night, before the rooster crows you will disown me three times. Matthew 26:34 The verb "aparneomai" (commonly translated "disowns") comes from the realm of legal and property transactions, and it means to renounce a relationship with someone or a claim upon property.

To deny Jesus is to treat him as a disregarded commodity, it is to treat Him as if he was something we had finished with, and we no longer want.
prayer: Father our denial of Jesus not only traps us but it also makes Jesus feel like a commodity.
